title: The Complete Guide to CBC Assessment Management for Kenyan Schools (2026)
h1: The Complete Guide to CBC Assessment Management for Kenyan Schools
description: A practical guide to CBC assessment management in Kenya: strands, rubrics, SBA uploads, KPSEA and KJSEA reports, transfers and term report cards.
author: SQUL Team
quickAnswer: CBC assessment management is the system a school uses to plan, capture, moderate, store and report assessment evidence under the Competency-Based Curriculum. In Kenya it covers learning areas, strands, sub-strands and performance levels from Grade 1 to Grade 9, the school-based assessment (SBA) uploaded to KNEC's CBA portal, and the reports that follow: term report cards, KPSEA at Grade 6 and KJSEA at Grade 9.
intro: CBC assessment management is the quiet engine behind every credible CBC report: the routines, records and checks that turn classroom evidence into a result a parent, a headteacher and KNEC can all trust. It sits inside the wider job of running a school, which is why the best [school management software in Kenya](/blog/best-school-management-software-kenya) treats assessment as a core record rather than an add-on. This guide is the hub for that work.

Most schools do not fail at CBC because teachers cannot assess. They fail because the evidence lives in a class workbook, the marks live in a spreadsheet, the SBA scores live on the KNEC portal, and the report card lives in a Word template that three people edit differently. By the last week of term, nobody can tell which version is true.

The fix is not a new template. It is a short, disciplined operating system: one learner record, one curriculum map, one evidence trail, one approval step, and reports generated from the same data. This guide explains that system, connects the ten practical guides in this cluster, and shows where a school management platform like SQUL fits — and where it does not.

sections.heading: What CBC assessment management actually means

blocks.text: CBC assessment management is the end-to-end handling of assessment data under the Competency-Based Curriculum. It starts with planning what evidence will be collected, runs through capturing and moderating that evidence, and ends with reports that parents, schools and KNEC can act on. Assessment itself — the professional judgement a teacher makes about a learner — is not the software's job. Keeping that judgement accurate, complete and retrievable is.

items: **Plan:** map learning areas to strands, sub-strands and the evidence that will show mastery.
**Capture:** record a performance level against the right learner, learning area, strand, term and teacher.
**Moderate:** compare levels across teachers and streams so the standard does not drift.
**Verify:** check that every candidate's school-based assessment (SBA) reached the KNEC CBA portal correctly.
**Report:** generate term report cards, school reports and parent conversations from the same record.

blocks.text: That is a data lifecycle, not a document. Once a school sees it that way, most of the term-end panic disappears: the report card is a view of the record, the KNEC upload is an export of the record, and the board report is a summary of the same record.

blocks.caption: Illustrative view: classroom evidence, the school record, the KNEC CBA portal and the final reports are four views of one assessment record — not four separate jobs.

sections.heading: The four records every CBC school must keep

blocks.text: A school can lose a term of assessment work through one broken laptop, one deleted column or one teacher who leaves without handing over. These four records are the minimum defence.

blocks.caption: The minimum CBC assessment record set.
rows: Name, UPI, admission number, KNEC assessment number, grade, stream
One record per learner, no duplicates
Learning areas, strands, sub-strands and expected evidence for the term
Level, date, task, teacher, strand and supporting evidence
Every level traceable to a task
What was uploaded, by whom, when, and what changed after review
Signed off before each KNEC deadline

blocks.title: If it only exists in one teacher's laptop, it is not a record
blocks.text: A record is something the school can retrieve, explain and defend after the teacher has left the room. That means a shared system, a backup, and an audit trail — not a WhatsApp attachment.

sections.heading: The CBC assessment year, term by term

blocks.text: CBC assessment runs on a rhythm, not a single exam week. School-based assessment is administered through the year, with projects and practical tasks typically concentrated in Term 2 and written tests in Term 3. National assessment sits at the end of the cycle: KPSEA for Grade 6 and KJSEA for Grade 9.

blocks.caption: Illustrative view: a CBC assessment calendar that puts classroom tasks, SBA uploads and national assessment on one timeline.

blocks.text: In the 2026 schedule, KNEC released Term 3 assessment tools for Grades 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8 on 28 September, with scores due by 23 October. Grade 6 and Grade 9 candidates were left out of that round so schools could prepare them for KPSEA and KJSEA. Dates move from year to year, so treat this as a pattern to copy, not a permanent calendar: confirm the current circular and download the tools from the [KNEC CBA portal](https://cba.knec.ac.ke).

blocks.title: Put the KNEC deadline on the same wall as the exam timetable
blocks.text: The most common SBA failure is not a corrupt file. It is a school that finished teaching, sat its end-term exams, closed for the holiday — and remembered the portal deadline afterwards.

sections.heading: Who owns what: roles and decision rights

blocks.text: CBC assessment fails when everyone assumes someone else is holding the spreadsheet. A simple split of responsibilities is enough, provided the same names appear on the term plan every term.

blocks.caption: A workable ownership model for a Kenyan school.
rows: Overall accuracy and timely KNEC compliance
Approves the final SBA upload and result release
Sets tasks, deadlines and moderation rules
Learner-level completeness and report card comments
Confirms the class record is complete
Controls portal access; cannot change levels
Reviews aggregate reports, never individual edits

blocks.title: Separate data entry from data approval
blocks.text: The person who types a score should not be the only person who approves the upload. A second pair of eyes is the cheapest data-quality control a school has.

sections.heading: KPSEA and KJSEA in plain English

blocks.text: KPSEA is the national assessment at the end of Grade 6. KJSEA is the national assessment at the end of Grade 9. Neither is a stand-alone exam score: school-based assessment accumulated over earlier grades contributes to the final result. That is why a school's assessment records matter long before the candidate sits the national paper.

blocks.caption: How the national assessment results are built (2026 guidance).
rows: SBA in Grades 4, 5 and 6 (60%) + national assessment (40%)
KPSEA (20%) + SBA in Grades 7 and 8 (20%) + Grade 9 national assessment (60%)

blocks.text: KJSEA reports four performance descriptors — Exceeding Expectations, Meeting Expectations, Approaching Expectations and Below Expectations — each subdivided into two, giving an eight-point scale from EE1 to BE2. It does not produce an aggregate score or a school mean, and KNEC has explicitly warned against ranking schools on it. Read [KNEC's explanation of the KJSEA grading scale](https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2025-12-15-knec-explains-new-kjsea-grading-system) before you brief parents or the board.

blocks.caption: Illustrative view: the weighting behind KPSEA and KJSEA, and the level-based reporting that replaces aggregate scores. The distribution shown is illustrative, not real school data.

blocks.title: Weightings are policy, not constants
blocks.text: The percentages above reflect KNEC guidance in 2026. Confirm the current circular before publishing a parent letter, and keep a dated copy of the guidance your school relied on.

sections.heading: From classroom evidence to KNEC upload to report card

blocks.text: The data flow is simple to describe and hard to keep clean. Each step should leave the record stronger, not create a second copy of it.

items.title: Plan the evidence
items.text: Agree the strands, sub-strands and tasks for the term. A teacher should never wonder what to assess in week nine.

items.title: Capture at the point of evidence
items.text: Enter the level while the task is fresh, with the date, strand and a note on the evidence used.

items.title: Moderate before locking
items.text: Compare a sample of learners across streams. If one teacher's ME looks like another's EE, fix the standard before the data leaves the school.

items.title: Lock the term
items.text: Freeze the assessment record so report cards and uploads come from a known version.

items.title: Upload and verify
items.text: Export the SBA scores, upload them to the KNEC CBA portal, then verify the upload against the school record.

items.title: Generate the reports
items.text: Print report cards, prepare the school report and brief parents from the same locked data.

blocks.text: The same record should produce at least four outputs: a learner report card, a class or stream analysis, a school-level summary for the board, and the SBA export for KNEC. If any of those is being rebuilt by hand, the school is paying for the same data twice.

blocks.caption: Illustrative view: a school CBA portal workspace for candidate registers, SBA upload status and downloadable reports. Portal labels change between releases — follow the current KNEC user manual for exact steps.

sections.heading: Where Excel breaks — and why it feels fine at first

blocks.text: Excel is not the enemy. It is a flexible, familiar tool that gets a school through its first term of CBC recording. The trouble starts when the workbook becomes the school's only source of truth and several people need to edit it at once.

blocks.caption: The failure modes that appear once a CBC workbook grows up.
rows: Grade 7 Maths final v3 (2).xlsx on three laptops
Reports produced from the wrong version
EE, E, Exceeding, 4, 75% in the same column
Some learners silently excluded from a totals row
Nobody knows who changed a level or when
Mail-merge into a Word template for each stream
Days of rework and format drift
The same scores typed into the CBA portal

blocks.title: Still on Excel this term?
blocks.text: You can survive one more term if you add a version owner, a locked column for levels and a second-person check before upload. The [CBC data entry mistakes guide](/blog/common-cbc-data-entry-mistakes) turns that into a checklist.

sections.heading: A term-by-term operating rhythm that holds

blocks.text: Assessment management is mostly calendar discipline. This is the rhythm we see work in schools running CBC across several streams and campuses.

blocks.caption: What must be true, and who checks it.
rows: Curriculum map, assessment tasks and report template agreed
Every learner and stream loaded; baseline evidence captured
Strand coverage reviewed; gaps and absentees flagged
All levels entered; moderation complete; evidence attached
SBA exported, uploaded and verified on the CBA portal
Report cards released; support plans and next-term targets set

blocks.text: A report is not trusted because it is printed on good paper. It is trusted because the numbers on it can be explained. That means the person presenting the report can trace a level back to a task, a strand and a teacher.

items: **Term report cards** for parents, generated from the locked learner record.
**KPSEA and KJSEA school reports** for the headteacher and board, read by learning area and level rather than a single mean.
**Class and stream analysis** for the DOS, showing where coverage or achievement is slipping.
**Parent conversations** that use the same evidence the teacher used, not a separate summary.
**Transfer records** that travel with a learner who moves mid-term.

blocks.text: Each of those has a dedicated guide below: [automatic term report cards](/blog/generate-cbc-term-report-cards-automatically), [KPSEA and KJSEA reports for headteachers](/blog/headteacher-guide-kpsea-kjsea-reports) and [KNEC CBA portal reports](/blog/knec-cba-portal-reports-guide).

Do not choose on the report card design. Choose on the data model behind it. A beautiful template cannot fix a record that never captured sub-strands, and a cheap tool that stores levels as free text will cost more in rework than it saves.

blocks.text: You need software to run CBC at scale — across streams, terms, teachers and a KNEC deadline — without rebuilding the same record four times.

faqs.question: What is CBC assessment management?
faqs.answer: It is the end-to-end handling of assessment data under the Competency-Based Curriculum: planning evidence, capturing performance levels against learning areas and strands, moderating across teachers, uploading school-based assessment to KNEC, and generating report cards and school reports from the same record.

faqs.question: Is CBA the same as CBC?
faqs.answer: No. CBC is the curriculum — what learners learn and the competencies they develop. CBA is the assessment framework used to judge that learning. In everyday Kenyan school language, people often use CBC and CBA interchangeably, but the distinction matters when you are describing records and reports.

faqs.question: What percentage of KPSEA and KJSEA comes from school-based assessment?
faqs.answer: Under the 2026 guidance, KPSEA combines SBA from Grades 4, 5 and 6 (60%) with the Grade 6 national assessment (40%). KJSEA combines KPSEA (20%), SBA from Grades 7 and 8 (20%) and the Grade 9 national assessment (60%). Confirm the current KNEC circular before relying on these weightings.

faqs.question: Does KJSEA have a mean score or school ranking?
faqs.answer: No. KJSEA reports performance levels by learning area on an eight-point scale from EE1 to BE2. KNEC has stated that it does not produce an aggregate score, a mean grade or a school mean score, and has warned against ranking schools on the results.

faqs.question: Who uploads SBA scores to the KNEC CBA portal?
faqs.answer: The school does, through its headteacher or a delegated portal administrator, using the school's CBA portal account. Teachers and the DOS prepare and verify the underlying records; the head remains accountable for what is uploaded.

faqs.question: Can a school manage CBC assessment without software?
faqs.answer: Yes, for a small school with one stream and a disciplined workbook. It becomes risky once several streams, teachers and terms are involved, because the report card, the KNEC upload and the board report are usually rebuilt by hand from the same data. Software is a scale decision more than a curriculum decision.

faqs.question: What records must move when a learner transfers mid-term?
faqs.answer: At minimum: the learner profile and UPI, the assessment history by learning area and strand, evidence samples, attendance, and the transfer letter. If the learner is a KPSEA or KJSEA candidate, confirm which school owns the assessment centre and the SBA upload before either side submits.
